title: Skin & Respiratory System
summary: Examine the body's outer barrier and the airway from nose to alveolus at microscope level.

lessons.title: Epidermis: Keratinocytes, Melanocytes & Layers

levels.kid:
Your skin has a top layer called the **epidermis**. It is like a brick wall that keeps germs out and water in.

The bricks are cells called **keratinocytes**. New bricks are made at the very bottom. They slowly move up to the top. On the way, they fill up with a tough material called **keratin**, the same stuff in your fingernails. By the time they reach the top, they are flat and no longer alive, like dry leaves. Then they flake off, and new ones take their place.

Other helper cells live here too. **Melanocytes** make **melanin**, a brown color that acts like a tiny umbrella against sunlight. Your outer skin replaces itself about once a month!
levels.hs:
The **epidermis** is the outermost layer of skin. Under the microscope it is a **stratified squamous keratinized epithelium**: many layers of cells, with flat cells at the surface covered in dead, keratin-filled cells. It has no blood vessels. It gets nutrients by diffusion from the dermis below.

Most epidermal cells are **keratinocytes**. They are born in the bottom layer and move upward, changing as they go. From deep to surface, the layers are:
- **Stratum basale**: one row of dividing stem cells on the basement membrane
- **Stratum spinosum**: cells joined by many connections called desmosomes, which look like "spines" on slides
- **Stratum granulosum**: cells with dark granules that help build the waterproof barrier
- **Stratum lucidum**: a clear layer found only in thick skin (palms and soles)
- **Stratum corneum**: flat dead cells packed with keratin, which flake away

A cell takes roughly a month to travel from base to shedding.

Three other cell types are present. **Melanocytes** in the basal layer make the pigment **melanin** and pass it to keratinocytes. **Langerhans cells** are immune sentinels. **Merkel cells** sense light touch.

Real example: people of different skin colors have about the same number of melanocytes. Darker skin comes from more and larger melanin granules, not more melanocytes.
levels.college:
The epidermis is a self-renewing stratified squamous keratinized epithelium derived from surface ectoderm. It sits on a basement membrane, and its rete ridges interlock with dermal papillae. It has no blood vessels, although free nerve endings reach into it.

**Keratinocyte differentiation (cornification)**, deep to superficial:
- **Basale**: cuboidal to columnar stem and transit-amplifying cells. **Hemidesmosomes** anchor them to the basement membrane through integrin α6β4. They express **keratins K5/K14**.
- **Spinosum**: polygonal cells that switch to **K1/K10**. Shrinkage during tissue processing pulls cells apart at their **desmosomes**, which produces the "prickle" appearance. Lamellar bodies begin to form here.
- **Granulosum**: basophilic **keratohyalin granules** containing profilaggrin and loricrin. **Lamellar bodies (Odland bodies)** release lipids, including ceramides, cholesterol and free fatty acids, into the space between cells.
- **Lucidum**: eosinophilic band seen in thick skin.
- **Corneum**: anucleate **corneocytes**. Each has a **cornified envelope** of cross-linked proteins, made by transglutaminase, surrounded by a lipid envelope.

Thick skin (palms and soles) has a massive corneum and a lucidum but no hair. Thin skin covers the rest of the body.

**Non-keratinocytes**:
- **Melanocytes** derive from the neural crest and sit in the basale. Each extends dendrites to about 36 keratinocytes, a unit called the **epidermal melanin unit**. Melanin is made in **melanosomes** from tyrosine by **tyrosinase**. Melanosomes are transferred to keratinocytes, where they cap the nucleus to shield DNA from UV.
- **Langerhans cells** are dendritic antigen-presenting cells of the spinosum. They contain **Birbeck granules** (langerin) and are CD1a+.
- **Merkel cells** sit in the basale and synapse with Aβ afferents to form slowly adapting mechanoreceptors.

In routine H&E stains, melanocytes and Langerhans cells look like "clear cells" with a pale halo around them.
levels.phd:
Epidermal homeostasis depends on basal progenitors that balance self-renewal against commitment. Lineage tracing by Clayton and colleagues (2007) challenged the classical model of epidermal proliferative units, in which slow stem cells feed transit-amplifying cells. Their data instead fit a single committed progenitor population with stochastic fate: symmetric and asymmetric divisions produce clone sizes that scale over time. Whether a distinct slow-cycling stem cell compartment also exists in interfollicular epidermis is still debated, and it may vary by body site.

**Transcriptional control**: **p63** (ΔNp63) is essential for stratification; p63-null mice lack an epidermis. **Notch** signalling drives exit into the spinous fate. **KLF4** and **GRHL3** are needed for terminal barrier formation. Calcium rises steeply from basale to granulosum, and this gradient triggers differentiation and the assembly of desmosomes and adherens junctions.

**Barrier biochemistry**: profilaggrin is dephosphorylated and cleaved into filaggrin monomers. Filaggrin aggregates keratin filaments, and its breakdown products (urocanic acid, pyrrolidone carboxylic acid) form "natural moisturizing factor" and help acidify the surface. **Transglutaminases 1, 3 and 5** cross-link involucrin, loricrin and SPRRs into the cornified envelope. Ceramides are covalently bound to involucrin to build the corneocyte lipid envelope. **Tight junctions** in the granulosum (claudin-1) form a second, paracellular barrier. The "bricks and mortar" model describes corneocytes as bricks and lamellar lipids as mortar.

**Melanogenesis**: α-MSH from keratinocyte POMC binds **MC1R** and raises cAMP, which activates **MITF** and induces tyrosinase, TYRP1 and DCT. UV damage triggers p53 to induce POMC in keratinocytes, which links DNA damage to tanning. Eumelanin (brown-black) is more photoprotective than pheomelanin (red-yellow). Pheomelanin may promote oxidative damage even without UV. MC1R loss-of-function variants shift production toward pheomelanin. Melanosomes mature through stages I to IV. How they are transferred to keratinocytes (cytophagocytosis, shed vesicles, exo/endocytosis) remains contested.

**Desmosomal cadherins** change across the layers. **Desmoglein 3** is concentrated in the lower layers and **desmoglein 1** in the upper layers, which matters for blistering disease patterns.
levels.expert:
Epidermal histology maps directly onto clinical pathology, and level of split, pattern and cell type drive diagnosis.

**Desmoglein compensation theory** (Amagai): pemphigus foliaceus (anti-Dsg1) splits in the subcorneal/granular layer, because Dsg3 protects the lower layers. Mucosal pemphigus vulgaris (anti-Dsg3) splits just above the basale in the mouth, where Dsg3 dominates. Once Dsg1 antibodies are also present, skin blisters suprabasally too, leaving a "tombstone" row of basal cells. Staphylococcal scalded skin syndrome and bullous impetigo cleave Dsg1 through exfoliative toxins and mimic foliaceus. Bullous pemphigoid targets the hemidesmosome proteins BP180 (collagen XVII) and BP230, giving a subepidermal blister.

**Keratin and barrier genetics**: KRT5/KRT14 mutations cause epidermolysis bullosa simplex, in which basal cells lyse under shear. KRT1/KRT10 mutations cause epidermolytic ichthyosis. FLG null variants are the strongest genetic risk factor for atopic dermatitis and underlie ichthyosis vulgaris, which shows a thinned or absent granular layer. TGM1 loss causes lamellar ichthyosis.

**Reading pathology terms**: hyperkeratosis is a thickened corneum. Parakeratosis means nuclei are retained in the corneum, as in psoriasis, where basal-to-corneum transit shortens to days. Acanthosis is a thickened spinosum. Spongiosis is fluid between keratinocytes (eczema). Acantholysis is loss of cohesion (pemphigus).

**Melanocyte pitfalls**: in H&E, keratinocytes with perinuclear halos can mimic melanocytes. Immunostains (SOX10, MelanA/MART-1, HMB-45, PRAME) separate lineages and help tell melanoma from benign nevi. Pagetoid upward spread of melanocytes is a red flag for melanoma in situ. Vitiligo is autoimmune, CD8+ T-cell–mediated loss of melanocytes. In albinism, melanocytes are present but tyrosinase or a melanosomal protein is defective. Langerhans cell histiocytosis shows CD1a+/langerin+ cells, often with BRAF V600E.

**Frontier and open questions**: single-cell atlases are redefining basal heterogeneity. Somatic mutation mapping (Martincorena, 2015) showed that sun-exposed normal eyelid skin carries many positively selected NOTCH1 and TP53 clones, which challenges the idea that a "driver mutation" means cancer. Barrier-repair therapies and biologics targeting IL-4/IL-13 restore filaggrin expression in atopic skin. For a neurosurgeon, the shared ectodermal and neural crest origins explain the skin signs of neurocutaneous syndromes: café-au-lait macules in NF1, hypomelanotic macules in tuberous sclerosis.

keyPoints: Epidermis is avascular stratified squamous keratinized epithelium
Layers deep to surface: basale, spinosum, granulosum, lucidum (thick skin), corneum
Keratinocytes switch keratins K5/K14 to K1/K10 as they differentiate
Keratohyalin (filaggrin) and lamellar bodies (lipids) build the barrier
Neural crest melanocytes transfer melanosomes that cap keratinocyte nuclei
Langerhans cells present antigen; Merkel cells sense light touch

test.q: Which epidermal layer contains the dividing stem cells?
test.explain: The basale is the single row of dividing cells on the basement membrane. The corneum holds dead cells that no longer divide.

test.q: The 'prickly' look of the stratum spinosum comes from:
test.explain: Cells shrink during processing but stay joined at desmosomes, which looks like spines.

test.q: The stratum lucidum is found mainly in the skin of:
test.explain: The stratum lucidum is a clear layer characteristic of thick skin on the palms and soles.

test.q: Melanocytes develop from which embryonic source?
test.explain: Melanocytes migrate from the neural crest. Keratinocytes come from surface ectoderm.

test.q: Darker skin color mainly reflects:
test.explain: Melanocyte numbers are similar across skin tones. Melanosome amount and size differ.

test.q: Which cell is the antigen-presenting cell of the epidermis?
test.explain: Langerhans cells are dendritic immune cells with Birbeck granules that present antigen in the epidermis. Merkel cells are touch receptors, melanocytes produce pigment, and corneocytes are dead keratinized cells.

test.q: Keratohyalin granules in the stratum granulosum contain:
test.explain: Keratohyalin holds profilaggrin and loricrin, which aggregate keratin and build the cornified envelope.

test.q: Basal keratinocytes mainly express which keratin pair?
test.explain: Basal cells express K5/K14. They switch to K1/K10 when they enter the spinosum.

test.q: Within keratinocytes, melanin granules are positioned to:
test.explain: Melanosomes form a supranuclear cap that protects DNA from UV radiation.

test.q: What is the outermost layer of dead, keratin-filled cells called (stratum ___)?
test.explain: The stratum corneum is made of anucleate corneocytes that are shed from the surface.

test.q: Melanin is made in organelles called ___.
test.explain: Tyrosinase inside melanosomes converts tyrosine into melanin.

test.q: The epidermis has no blood vessels, so it is described as ___.
test.explain: Nutrients diffuse up from dermal capillaries.

kidTest.q: What is the top layer of your skin called?
kidTest.explain: The epidermis is the outer layer of skin.

kidTest.q: What does melanin do?
kidTest.explain: Melanin is a color that works like an umbrella against the sun.

kidTest.q: Where are new skin cells made?
kidTest.explain: New cells start at the bottom and move up.

kidTest.q: What happens to cells at the top of the skin?
kidTest.explain: Old flat cells at the top flake away.

kidTest.q: The tough stuff in skin cells and fingernails is k _ _ _ _ _ _.
kidTest.explain: Keratin makes skin cells and nails tough.

advancedTest.q: A patient has antibodies only to desmoglein 1. Where would blisters most likely form?
advancedTest.explain: Dsg1 dominates the upper epidermis, and Dsg3 protects the deeper layers, so the split is superficial, as in pemphigus foliaceus.

advancedTest.q: Clayton et al.'s epidermal clone-size data were best explained by:
choices: Melanocytes acting as hidden epidermal stem cells
One progenitor pool with stochastic fate choice
Fixed proliferative units with a slow stem cell
Dedifferentiation of corneocytes into basal cells
advancedTest.explain: Scaling clone-size distributions fit a single committed progenitor population with random division outcomes. This challenged the epidermal proliferative unit model.

advancedTest.q: Why do FLG null variants predispose to atopic dermatitis?
choices: They block melanosome transfer to keratinocytes
They abolish hemidesmosome anchoring to the basement membrane
They weaken keratin aggregation and moisturizing factor
They prevent Langerhans cells from leaving the skin
advancedTest.explain: Filaggrin aggregates keratin, and its breakdown yields natural moisturizing factor. Losing it impairs the barrier, which allows allergen entry.

advancedTest.q: A scalp biopsy shows nuclei retained in the stratum corneum. This finding:
choices: Shows spongiosis from fluid between cells
Is hyperkeratosis, a thick but normal corneum
Suggests accelerated transit, as in psoriasis
advancedTest.explain: Parakeratosis means nuclei are retained because keratinocytes reach the surface too quickly to finish cornifying, which is classic for psoriasis.

lessons.title: Dermis, Hair Follicles & Skin Glands

levels.kid:
Under the thin top layer of your skin is a thicker layer called the **dermis**. Think of it like the strong cloth under the paint on a wall. It is full of stretchy, tough threads that let your skin bend and bounce back.

The dermis holds lots of tiny helpers:
- **Hair follicles**, little pockets where hairs grow.
- **Sweat glands**, tiny coiled tubes that make sweat to cool you down.
- **Oil glands**, which make oil to keep skin and hair soft.

Each hair has a tiny muscle attached. When you feel cold or scared, the muscle pulls the hair up. That gives you goosebumps!

The dermis also has blood vessels and nerves, so you can feel a soft touch or a sharp poke.
levels.hs:
Beneath the epidermis lies the **dermis**, a layer of connective tissue that gives skin its strength and stretch. It has two parts:
- The **papillary dermis**, a thin top layer of loose connective tissue. It pushes up into the epidermis in finger-like bumps called **dermal papillae**, which help glue the layers together and carry tiny blood vessels.
- The **reticular dermis**, a thick deeper layer of dense irregular connective tissue packed with **collagen** (for strength) and **elastic fibers** (for recoil).

The dermis houses the **skin appendages**:
- **Hair follicles**: tubes of epithelium that dip down into the dermis. At the base, a bulb of dividing cells wraps around a dermal papilla that feeds it.
- **Sebaceous glands**: oil glands that empty into hair follicles. They release **sebum** by whole cells breaking apart.
- **Eccrine sweat glands**: found almost everywhere, opening directly onto the skin surface. They make watery sweat for cooling.
- **Apocrine sweat glands**: in the armpits and groin, emptying into hair follicles. Bacteria break down their secretion, which causes body odor.
- **Arrector pili**: small smooth muscles that raise hairs, causing goosebumps.

A real example: **acne** starts when sebum and shed cells plug a follicle, and bacteria such as *Cutibacterium acnes* trigger inflammation.
levels.college:
The dermis is a connective tissue layer, roughly 1 to 4 mm thick depending on site, made mainly by **fibroblasts**. It is separated from the epidermis by a basement membrane, and below it lies the **hypodermis** (subcutis), which is mostly adipose tissue.

**Layers**
- **Papillary dermis**: loose areolar tissue with fine type I and type III collagen, capillary loops and **Meissner corpuscles** (light touch). Dermal papillae interlock with epidermal rete ridges, which resists shear.
- **Reticular dermis**: dense irregular connective tissue with coarse type I collagen bundles and elastic fibers. The dominant orientation of the bundles creates **Langer's (cleavage) lines**. Deep in the dermis and hypodermis sit **Pacinian corpuscles** (vibration and pressure).

**Hair follicle anatomy** (from deep to superficial)
- **Bulb**: **matrix** cells around the **dermal papilla** divide quickly, and melanocytes there add pigment to the hair.
- **Inner root sheath** (Henle, Huxley and cuticle layers) and **outer root sheath** (continuous with the epidermis), surrounded by a connective tissue **glassy membrane**.
- **Bulge**: where the arrector pili inserts. It holds follicle stem cells.
- **Isthmus** and **infundibulum**: the sebaceous duct opens at the junction between them.

**Glands and secretion modes**
- **Sebaceous**: **holocrine**. Whole cells fill with lipid and disintegrate. Under H&E the cells look pale and foamy.
- **Eccrine**: **merocrine** (exocytosis). The coiled secretory part has clear cells (water and electrolytes), dark cells (glycoproteins) and myoepithelial cells. The duct, lined by a double layer of cuboidal cells that stain darker, reabsorbs Na+ and Cl−. They are cholinergic, sympathetic.
- **Apocrine**: wide lumen, single layer of eosinophilic cells with apical snouts. Despite the name, secretion is largely merocrine. They become active at puberty.

Modified apocrine glands include the **ceruminous** glands of the ear canal and the **Moll** glands of the eyelid.
levels.phd:
The hair follicle is a self-renewing mini-organ that cycles through **anagen** (growth, lasting years on the scalp), **catagen** (regression by apoptosis, about 2 to 3 weeks) and **telogen** (rest, roughly 3 months). The **bulge** in the outer root sheath contains slow-cycling stem cells, marked by **Keratin 15**, **CD34** (in mouse) and **Lgr5** in the lower bulge/secondary germ. Cotsarelis, Sun and Lavker's 1990 label-retaining cell experiments located these stem cells. Lineage tracing later showed that bulge cells feed both the follicle and, after wounding, the interfollicular epidermis, although they do not maintain the epidermis at steady state.

Anagen entry depends on signals from the **dermal papilla**: **Wnt/β-catenin** activation, **Sonic hedgehog** from the matrix, and relief of **BMP** inhibition. Intradermal adipocyte precursors supply PDGF-A, which helps start the cycle. Plikus and colleagues showed that BMP rhythms in the dermal macroenvironment synchronize whole follicle populations, which explains coordinated hair waves in mice.

The dermal papilla controls follicle identity. Classic recombination studies (Jahoda, Oliver, Reynolds) showed that transplanted papilla cells can induce new follicles. Papilla cell volume correlates with hair shaft size, and androgen-driven papilla shrinkage underlies follicle miniaturization in **androgenetic alopecia**, mediated by 5α-reductase type 2 and dihydrotestosterone.

**Sebocytes** come from Blimp1- and Lrig1-positive progenitors near the infundibulum. They accumulate triglycerides, wax esters and **squalene** under PPARγ control, then undergo a specialized lipid-laden holocrine cell death. Sebaceous output is strongly androgen-dependent.

**Eccrine physiology**: postganglionic sympathetic fibers release acetylcholine onto M3 receptors. Clear cells secrete an isotonic primary fluid through basolateral NKCC1 and apical Cl− channels (TMEM16A, possibly CFTR). Duct cells then reabsorb NaCl through **ENaC** and **CFTR**, making the sweat hypotonic. Because CFTR is defective in cystic fibrosis, Cl− cannot be reabsorbed, which is the basis of the diagnostic **sweat chloride test**. Humans have about 2 to 4 million eccrine glands, an unusually high density among primates, and the transcription factor **Engrailed-1** sets how many form.
levels.expert:
Dermal pathology is read largely by spatial pattern. Dermatopathologists sort inflammatory infiltrates into superficial perivascular, superficial and deep perivascular, interface, nodular/diffuse, panniculitic, or folliculocentric patterns. The depth of the infiltrate and its relation to appendages often point to the diagnosis before any cytology is assessed. Examples include superficial and deep perivascular lymphocytes with mucin in lupus, and peri-eccrine lymphocytes, also seen in lupus and lichen striatus.

**Alopecia work-up** depends on horizontal (Headington) sectioning of a 4 mm punch biopsy. This allows follicles to be counted and terminal-to-vellus and anagen-to-telogen ratios to be calculated.
- Non-scarring: androgenetic alopecia (miniaturization, raised vellus counts); alopecia areata (peribulbar "swarm of bees" lymphocytes around anagen bulbs, reflecting loss of bulb immune privilege, with CD8+ NKG2D+ T cells and IFN-γ/JAK signaling). This understanding led to approval of the JAK inhibitors baricitinib, ritlecitinib and deuruxolitinib.
- Scarring: lichen planopilaris and frontal fibrosing alopecia attack the **bulge**. Permanent loss follows from stem cell destruction, which is why early diagnosis matters.

**Adnexal neoplasms** recapitulate normal structures. Trichoepithelioma and trichoblastoma resemble follicular germinative cells, sebaceous adenoma resembles sebaceous lobules, and poroma and hidradenoma resemble the eccrine duct. A practical pitfall is that basal cell carcinoma and trichoepithelioma can look alike. Stromal retraction clefts, mucin and myxoid stroma favor BCC; papillary mesenchymal bodies and CK20-positive Merkel cells favor trichoepithelioma. Multiple sebaceous neoplasms raise suspicion for **Muir-Torre syndrome** (mismatch repair deficiency), so screening for visceral malignancy is needed.

**Hidradenitis suppurativa** is a disease of follicular occlusion, not primarily of apocrine glands, as was once believed. IL-17 is a key driver, and the anti-IL-17 antibodies secukinumab and bimekizumab are now approved.

In surgery, incisions placed along Langer's/relaxed skin tension lines heal with less tension. Neurosurgeons often use scalp incisions behind the hairline, made bevelled parallel to the follicles to avoid transecting them.

Open questions include whether follicles can regenerate in adult humans (wound-induced neogenesis is robust in mice but limited in humans), building follicle-bearing skin organoids from stem cells (Lee and Koehler, 2020), and dermal fibroblast heterogeneity: distinct papillary and reticular lineages appear to determine whether skin scars or regenerates.

keyPoints: Dermis = papillary (loose) + reticular (dense irregular, type I collagen) layers
Hair follicle: bulb with matrix around a dermal papilla; bulge holds stem cells
Sebaceous glands are holocrine and empty into follicles
Eccrine glands are merocrine, open on the skin, and the duct reabsorbs NaCl
Apocrine glands (axilla, groin) empty into follicles and activate at puberty
Hair cycle: anagen, catagen, telogen; scarring alopecia destroys the bulge

test.q: Which layer of the dermis is made of dense irregular connective tissue?
test.explain: The reticular dermis is thick dense irregular tissue with coarse type I collagen. The papillary dermis is loose tissue.

test.q: How do sebaceous glands release their product?
test.explain: Sebocytes fill with lipid and disintegrate, which is holocrine secretion.

test.q: Where do follicle stem cells mainly reside?
test.explain: The bulge, where the arrector pili inserts, holds the slow-cycling follicle stem cells.

test.q: What does the eccrine sweat duct do to the primary sweat?
test.explain: Duct cells reabsorb NaCl through ENaC and CFTR, which makes sweat hypotonic.

test.q: Apocrine sweat glands differ from eccrine glands because they:
choices: Are spread over most body areas
Open directly onto the skin surface
test.explain: Apocrine glands empty into follicles in the axilla and groin. Eccrine glands open onto the surface and are found almost everywhere.

test.q: The arrector pili muscle is made of which tissue?
test.explain: Arrector pili are small smooth muscles that raise hairs and cause goosebumps.

test.q: Which receptor detects light touch in the papillary dermis?
test.explain: Meissner corpuscles sit in dermal papillae. Pacinian corpuscles lie deeper and sense vibration.

test.q: Under H&E, sebaceous gland cells typically look:
test.explain: Stored lipid dissolves during processing, leaving pale, foamy cells. Apical snouts belong to apocrine cells.

test.q: What is the main nerve signal that drives eccrine sweating?
test.explain: Eccrine glands are innervated by sympathetic fibers that unusually release acetylcholine onto M3 receptors.

test.q: The active growth phase of the hair cycle is called ___.
test.explain: Anagen is growth, catagen is regression and telogen is rest.

test.q: What oily product do sebaceous glands secrete?
test.explain: Sebum is a mixture of triglycerides, wax esters and squalene.

test.q: Lines of dominant collagen orientation in the dermis are called ___ lines.
test.explain: Langer's (cleavage) lines guide surgical incisions.

kidTest.q: What is the dermis?
choices: A tiny bone inside the ear
The hard outer part of a nail
A thick layer under the top skin
kidTest.explain: The dermis lies under the thin top layer of skin.

kidTest.q: What does sweat do for you?
kidTest.explain: Sweat cools your body.

kidTest.q: What causes goosebumps?
kidTest.explain: Little muscles pull hairs up when you feel cold or scared.

kidTest.q: Where do hairs grow from?
kidTest.explain: Hair follicles are little pockets where hairs grow.

kidTest.q: Skin glands make this to keep skin soft: o _ _
kidTest.explain: Oil glands keep skin and hair soft.

advancedTest.q: Why does cystic fibrosis raise sweat chloride levels?
choices: Clear cells secrete a much larger volume of fluid
Apocrine glands replace the eccrine glands
Ductal Cl− reabsorption through CFTR is impaired
Holocrine secretion adds chloride-rich cell debris
advancedTest.explain: Primary sweat is isotonic. Without functional CFTR, the duct cannot reabsorb Cl−, so salty sweat reaches the skin.

advancedTest.q: Why is lichen planopilaris permanent but alopecia areata often reversible?
choices: Alopecia areata acts on the hypodermis
Lichen planopilaris targets bulge stem cells
Lichen planopilaris attacks the sebaceous ducts
advancedTest.explain: Destroying the bulge removes follicle stem cells and causes scarring. Areata attacks anagen bulbs but preserves the bulge.

advancedTest.q: Transplanted dermal papilla cells inducing new follicles best supports which idea?
choices: Matrix cells set hair identity without help
Follicles arise mainly from sebocyte progenitors
Hair growth depends on eccrine duct signaling
advancedTest.explain: Recombination studies show the dermal papilla, a mesenchymal component, can instruct epithelium to form follicles.

advancedTest.q: A lesion that looks like BCC has papillary mesenchymal bodies and CK20+ Merkel cells. This favors:
advancedTest.explain: Papillary mesenchymal bodies and Merkel cells favor trichoepithelioma. Retraction clefts and mucin favor BCC.

lessons.title: Nasal Cavity & Olfactory Epithelium

levels.kid:
Your nose is more than two holes! Just inside, the air passes stiff little hairs that catch dust, like a doormat catching mud.

Deeper in, the walls are covered with a wet, sticky layer called **mucus**. Tiny hairs called **cilia** wave like a crowd doing the wave at a stadium. They sweep the dirty mucus to the back of your throat, where you swallow it without noticing.

The inside of your nose also warms the air, like a little heater, before it reaches your lungs.

High up in the roof of your nose is a small, special patch for **smelling**. It has nerve cells that touch the air. When a smell floats by, they send a message to your brain: "Cookies!"
levels.hs:
The **nasal cavity** is the first part of the airway. Under the microscope it has three zones.

- **Vestibule**: the entrance just inside the nostrils. It is lined with skin (**stratified squamous epithelium**) and has coarse hairs called **vibrissae** that trap large particles.
- **Respiratory region**: most of the cavity. It is lined with **respiratory epithelium**, which is pseudostratified ciliated columnar epithelium with **goblet cells**. "Pseudostratified" means it looks layered, but every cell touches the basement membrane. Goblet cells make mucus. Cilia beat to move it toward the throat. Bony shelves called **conchae** (turbinates) stir the air so it touches more of this surface. A rich bed of blood vessels underneath warms and moistens the air.
- **Olfactory region**: a small patch in the roof of the cavity, about the size of a postage stamp on each side. It holds **olfactory epithelium**, the tissue that detects smell.

Olfactory epithelium has three main cell types:
- **Olfactory receptor neurons**, nerve cells whose tips poke into the mucus
- **Supporting (sustentacular) cells**
- **Basal cells**, stem cells that make new neurons

A real example: when you have a cold, swollen tissue and extra mucus block air from reaching the olfactory patch. That is why food tastes bland. Much of "flavor" is actually smell.
levels.college:
**Regional histology of the nasal cavity**
- **Vestibule**: keratinized stratified squamous epithelium that continues from the facial skin, with vibrissae, sebaceous glands and sweat glands. Deeper in, it shifts to nonkeratinized epithelium and then to respiratory epithelium.
- **Respiratory region**: pseudostratified ciliated columnar epithelium. It contains ciliated cells, goblet cells, brush cells and basal cells. The lamina propria holds seromucous glands and lymphoid tissue (part of mucosa-associated lymphoid tissue). Over the conchae there are thin-walled **venous sinuses**, or swell bodies, that warm the air. These erectile-like sinuses swell on one side and then the other in a **nasal cycle** lasting a few hours. Kiesselbach's plexus on the anterior septum is the usual source of nosebleeds.
- **Mucociliary clearance**: a watery periciliary layer lets the cilia beat beneath a gel mucus blanket. The beat sweeps trapped particles back toward the nasopharynx.

**Olfactory epithelium** lies on the cribriform plate, the superior concha and the upper septum. It is tall pseudostratified columnar epithelium and has **no goblet cells**.
- **Olfactory sensory neurons (OSNs)** are bipolar neurons. Each one has a dendrite ending in a swollen **olfactory vesicle (knob)** that carries long, nonmotile cilia lying in the mucus. Odorant receptors sit on these cilia. The unmyelinated axons gather into **fila olfactoria**, pass through the cribriform plate and synapse in the olfactory bulb (cranial nerve I).
- **Sustentacular cells** are tall support cells with microvilli. They detoxify odorants and other chemicals.
- **Basal cells** come in two kinds: **horizontal basal cells**, which are reserve stem cells, and **globose basal cells**, which actively make new neurons. OSNs turn over continuously, on a timescale of weeks to months.
- **Bowman's glands** in the lamina propria secrete a serous fluid. This fluid dissolves odorants and constantly washes them away so new odors can be detected.

The olfactory mucosa is typically yellowish-brown from pigment, unlike the pink respiratory mucosa.
levels.phd:
**Odorant transduction.** Buck and Axel (1991; Nobel Prize 2004) discovered the odorant receptor (OR) gene family. These are class A GPCRs. Humans have about 400 intact OR genes and many pseudogenes; mice have about 1,100 functional ORs. Binding of an odorant activates **G_olf**, which stimulates **adenylyl cyclase III**. The resulting cAMP opens **CNGA2/CNGA4/CNGB1b** cyclic nucleotide-gated channels, letting Na⁺ and Ca²⁺ enter. Unusually, OSNs keep a high internal Cl⁻ concentration, so Ca²⁺ then opens **ANO2 (TMEM16B)** Ca²⁺-activated Cl⁻ channels. Chloride flows *out*, which amplifies depolarization. Adaptation comes from Ca²⁺/calmodulin lowering the CNG channels' sensitivity to cAMP, and from PDE1C breaking down cAMP.

**One neuron, one receptor.** Each OSN expresses a single OR allele, chosen stochastically. This choice depends on interchromosomal enhancer hubs (Greek Islands) and on heterochromatin silencing. An unfolded-protein feedback signal through ATF5 locks in the chosen receptor and stops further switching. OSNs expressing the same OR are scattered within broad zones of the epithelium. Their axons, however, converge onto about two **glomeruli** per bulb. The OR protein itself, together with cAMP-dependent guidance cues (neuropilin-1, Sema3A), sets where the axons go. Because each odor activates a combination of receptors, this produces a combinatorial code.

**Glia and regeneration.** **Olfactory ensheathing cells** wrap bundles of axons in the lamina propria. They combine features of Schwann cells and astrocytes. Globose basal cells divide (Ascl1⁺ → Neurog1⁺) to replace OSNs during normal turnover. Horizontal basal cells (Krt5⁺, p63⁺) stay dormant until severe injury, when loss of p63 releases them to rebuild every cell type.

**Nuance.** Most respiratory epithelial cells and sustentacular cells express **ACE2 and TMPRSS2**, while OSNs largely do not. This explains why SARS-CoV-2 anosmia is attributed mainly to damage of support cells and inflammation, not direct infection of the neurons. How the receptors collectively code odor percepts is still debated. Psychophysical estimates of how many odors humans can discriminate range widely, and the "one trillion odors" figure has been criticized on statistical grounds.
levels.expert:
**Clinical histopathology of the nasal mucosa**
- **Squamous metaplasia** of respiratory epithelium happens wherever airflow dries the surface or irritates it chronically, such as the anterior inferior turbinate, smokers, and a septal deviation. Biopsy reports should interpret it in light of the site.
- **Chronic rhinosinusitis with nasal polyps** shows a type 2, eosinophil-rich, edematous stroma and a thickened basement membrane. This biology underpins treatment with biologics against IL-4Rα, IL-5 and IgE. Neutrophil-dominant polyps (more common in some Asian cohorts) respond differently.
- **Primary ciliary dyskinesia**: nasal brushings examined by electron microscopy can show defects in dynein arms or the central apparatus. However, about 30% of cases have normal ultrastructure (for example, *DNAH11*), so high-speed video analysis and genetics are needed. **Nasal nitric oxide** measurement is a useful screening test. Kartagener syndrome adds situs inversus.

**Neurosurgical relevance**
- **Olfactory neuroblastoma (esthesioneuroblastoma)** arises from olfactory epithelium near the cribriform plate. Histology shows small round blue cells in lobules with neurofibrillary matrix, Homer Wright rosettes, and S100⁺ sustentacular cells at the edges. Hyams grading and Kadish staging guide treatment, which is increasingly endoscopic endonasal resection. The key differentials are SNUC, NUT carcinoma and SMARCB1-deficient carcinoma.
- **Olfactory groove meningiomas** and anterior skull base approaches put smell at risk. Surgeons try to preserve the olfactory strip and filaments where possible.
- **CSF rhinorrhea** after trauma or surgery happens because the cribriform plate is perforated; β2-transferrin confirms the fluid is CSF. The filaments' perineural sheaths are also a route from the nose into the subarachnoid space. This is relevant to *Naegleria fowleri* meningoencephalitis and to research on intranasal delivery of drugs to the CNS.

**Pitfalls**: Biopsies often miss olfactory epithelium, because it is patchy and increasingly replaced by respiratory epithelium with age. A biopsy with no OSNs therefore does not prove anosmia has a neural cause.

**Frontiers**: Single-cell atlases of the human olfactory mucosa now map horizontal basal cell activation states. Smell loss (hyposmia) is a prodromal marker of Parkinson's disease, and α-synuclein seeding assays on olfactory mucosa swabs (RT-QuIC) are being studied as a diagnostic test. Researchers are also exploring olfactory ensheathing cell grafts for spinal cord injury, but trial results have been modest.

**Open question**: why does human OSN regeneration fail with aging and after viral injury?

Respiratory region: pseudostratified ciliated columnar epithelium with goblet cells
Conchae and venous sinuses warm, humidify and filter air
Olfactory epithelium: OSNs, sustentacular cells, basal cells, and no goblet cells
Bowman's glands secrete serous fluid that dissolves and clears odorants
OSN axons cross the cribriform plate as cranial nerve I and are replaced from basal cells

lessons.title: Conducting Airways: Trachea to Bronchioles

levels.kid:
When you breathe in, air travels down a tube in your neck called the **trachea**, or windpipe. It splits into two smaller tubes, one for each lung. Those tubes keep splitting, like the branches of an upside-down tree.

The windpipe has stiff rings shaped like the letter C. They keep the tube open, the way the rings in a vacuum cleaner hose stop it from squashing flat.

The inside is lined with sticky **mucus** and tiny hairs called **cilia**. The mucus catches dust and germs. The cilia wave together like a crowd doing "the wave" at a stadium, sweeping the dirty mucus up to your throat so you can swallow or cough it away.

The smallest branches have no rings at all. Muscle and stretchy tissue hold them open instead.
levels.hs:
The **conducting airways** carry air to the lungs but do not exchange gas. They warm, moisten and clean the air on its way down.

The **trachea** is lined by **respiratory epithelium**. Its full name is **pseudostratified ciliated columnar epithelium**. It looks layered because the nuclei sit at different heights, but every cell actually touches the basement membrane. Its main cells are:
- **Ciliated cells**, which beat mucus upward toward the throat
- **Goblet cells**, which make mucus
- **Basal cells**, stem cells that replace damaged cells

Below the epithelium lie mucous glands. Deeper still are 16-20 **C-shaped rings of hyaline cartilage**. The open back of each "C" faces the esophagus and is closed by the **trachealis** smooth muscle.

The trachea divides into the **bronchi**. As the branches get smaller, a few things happen:
- Cartilage breaks up into scattered plates.
- Smooth muscle becomes more noticeable.
- The epithelium gets shorter, and the number of goblet cells falls.

**Bronchioles** are less than about 1 mm across. They have no cartilage and no glands, and they are lined by club cells.

This cleaning system is called the **mucociliary escalator**. Smoking paralyzes and destroys cilia. That is why smokers develop a "smoker's cough": coughing is the only way left to clear mucus.
levels.college:
**Wall layers of the trachea**:
- **Mucosa**: respiratory epithelium on a notably thick basement membrane, plus a lamina propria rich in elastic fibers and immune cells. This includes bronchus-associated lymphoid tissue.
- **Submucosa**: seromucous glands.
- **Cartilaginous layer**: C-rings of hyaline cartilage, with the trachealis muscle bridging the posterior gap. The trachealis contracts during coughing to narrow the lumen and increase airflow velocity.
- **Adventitia**: loose connective tissue that anchors the trachea to nearby structures.

**Cell types in respiratory epithelium**:
- **Ciliated cells** are the most numerous. Each carries about 200-300 motile cilia with the **9+2 axoneme**, powered by dynein arms.
- **Goblet cells** secrete mucins, mainly MUC5AC and MUC5B.
- **Basal cells** are the progenitors.
- **Brush cells** are chemosensory.
- **Neuroendocrine (Kulchitsky) cells** are small granule cells.

**Mucus layers**: mucus floats on a thin watery **periciliary layer**, which lets cilia beat freely. The ion channel **CFTR** helps keep this layer hydrated.

**Bronchi**:
- Intrapulmonary bronchi have irregular cartilage plates instead of rings.
- A continuous spiral layer of smooth muscle lies between the mucosa and the cartilage.
- On a slide, the mucosa often looks folded because the smooth muscle contracts after death.

**Bronchioles** (under about 1 mm):
- No cartilage, no glands, and few or no goblet cells.
- The epithelium thins from simple columnar to simple cuboidal.
- Smooth muscle is relatively prominent, which is why bronchospasm in asthma has such an effect here.
- **Club cells** (formerly Clara cells) are dome-shaped cells that secrete surfactant-like proteins and club cell secretory protein (CC16). They also detoxify inhaled compounds using cytochrome P450 enzymes and act as progenitors.

**Terminal bronchioles** are the last purely conducting segment. Distal to them, respiratory bronchioles have alveoli budding from their walls; those belong to the next lesson.
levels.phd:
**Airway branching and resistance**: the airway tree branches dichotomously over about 23 generations (Weibel's model). Generations 0-16 are conducting and form the anatomical dead space, about 150 mL in adults. Because the total cross-sectional area expands enormously with each generation, most airway resistance sits in the medium bronchi. The small airways (under 2 mm) form a physiological "quiet zone." Considerable small-airway disease can therefore accumulate before spirometry becomes abnormal.

**How cilia beat**: ciliary beating is metachronal (in coordinated waves) at about 10-15 Hz.
- Outer dynein arms (e.g., DNAH5) drive the power of the beat; inner arms shape the waveform.
- Radial spokes and the central pair regulate the beat.
- Mutations in these components cause **primary ciliary dyskinesia**: chronic sinusitis and bronchiectasis.
- In Kartagener syndrome, situs inversus is added, because nodal cilia that set left-right asymmetry are also dysfunctional.
- Beat frequency rises with cAMP signaling and with Ca2+ signaling.

**The two-layer model of mucus** (Button and Boucher, 2012): the periciliary layer is not plain watery fluid. It is a brush of tethered mucins (MUC1, MUC4, MUC16) that excludes secreted mucins. Clearance works when the osmotic pressure of the mucus layer stays below that of the brush. In cystic fibrosis, loss of CFTR-mediated chloride and bicarbonate secretion has two effects:
- It dehydrates the airway surface.
- It impairs mucin unpacking.
Mucus then concentrates, the brush collapses, and clearance fails.

**Cell lineages**: lineage tracing shows a hierarchy.
- **Basal cells** (KRT5+, TP63+) self-renew and generate secretory and ciliated cells. Notch signaling biases them toward secretory fates; FOXJ1 drives the ciliated program.
- **Club cells** (SCGB1A1+) repopulate the bronchiolar epithelium after injury.
- Variant club cells that resist naphthalene, located near neuroendocrine bodies and bronchoalveolar duct junctions, act as reserve stem cells.
- Single-cell atlases in 2018 (Montoro; Plasschaert) identified the **pulmonary ionocyte** (FOXI1+). Although rare, it expresses most of the airway's CFTR transcript, which reshaped models of CF pathogenesis.

**Remodeling in asthma**: airway remodeling includes subepithelial collagen thickening beneath the true basement membrane, goblet cell metaplasia driven by IL-13 through STAT6 and SPDEF, smooth muscle hypertrophy and hyperplasia, and submucosal gland enlargement.
levels.expert:
**Biopsy interpretation**: in endobronchial biopsies, the **reticular basement membrane** normally measures about 5-8 µm thick. Thickening is a reproducible marker of asthma, but it is not specific: it also appears in eosinophilic bronchitis. Two common pitfalls:
- **Tangential sectioning** falsely thickens the basement membrane.
- **Squamous metaplasia** in smokers can mimic a dysplastic precursor.

Smokers' airways may also show basal cell hyperplasia and goblet cell hyperplasia. These lesions lie on a continuum toward squamous carcinoma in situ, a central airway lesion. Adenocarcinoma, by contrast, arises more peripherally.

**Diagnosing primary ciliary dyskinesia**: this needs combined testing, because no single test is sufficient:
- **Nasal nitric oxide** screening, which is low in PCD
- High-speed video microscopy analysis of the ciliary beat
- Transmission electron microscopy of the axoneme
- Genetics
About 30% of PCD cases have normal ultrastructure on electron microscopy (for example, DNAH11 variants). Secondary dyskinesia after a viral infection causes false positives, so samples are often re-examined after culture at an air-liquid interface.

**Bronchiolar disease**: obliterative (constrictive) bronchiolitis follows lung transplantation (it is the bronchiolitis obliterans syndrome phenotype of chronic lung allograft dysfunction), as well as diacetyl exposure ("popcorn lung") and military burn-pit exposure. It is notoriously patchy. Transbronchial biopsy is insensitive, and diagnosis rests on CT air trapping and physiology. Elastic stains highlight scarred residual bronchioles beside unaccompanied pulmonary arteries; an artery without its expected companion airway is a classic clue.

**Therapeutic advances**:
- CFTR modulators (elexacaftor-tezacaftor-ivacaftor) restore surface hydration in eligible genotypes and have transformed CF prognosis.
- Dupilumab, which blocks the IL-4 and IL-13 receptor, reduces mucus plugging in type 2 asthma.
- Bronchial thermoplasty ablates airway smooth muscle; its long-term role remains debated.

**Open questions**:
- How ionocyte density relates to disease severity.
- Whether basal cell clones carrying smoking-induced mutations persist after quitting. Sequencing work by Yoshida and colleagues (2020) found that ex-smokers had more near-normal, mutation-poor cells, consistent with replenishment from protected stem cells.
- How tracheal regenerative grafts can avoid repeating the failures of seeded scaffolds.

**Neurosurgical relevance**: the cough reflex depends on vagal afferents and on brainstem integration. Airway protection is therefore a key concern after posterior fossa and lower cranial nerve surgery.

keyPoints: Conducting airways clean, warm and humidify air but do not exchange gas
Respiratory epithelium is pseudostratified ciliated columnar with goblet and basal cells
Trachea has C-shaped hyaline cartilage rings closed posteriorly by trachealis muscle

Bronchioles lack cartilage and glands; club cells replace goblet cells

lessons.title: Alveoli & the Blood–Air Barrier

levels.kid:
Deep inside your lungs are millions of tiny air bubbles called **alveoli**. They look a bit like bunches of grapes at the ends of thin tubes.

Each bubble is wrapped in a net of tiny blood tubes. The wall between the air and the blood is super thin, much thinner than a soap bubble's skin is wide to your eye. That lets oxygen slip from the air into your blood, and carbon dioxide slip out so you can breathe it away.

Some cells in the bubble walls make a slippery soap-like liquid. It stops the bubbles from squishing flat when you breathe out. Little cleaner cells also crawl around inside, eating dust that sneaks in.
levels.hs:
The airways end in tiny sacs called **alveoli** (singular: alveolus). An adult has roughly 300-500 million of them, giving a gas-exchange surface of about 70-100 square meters, around the size of a badminton court.

The alveolar wall is lined by two kinds of cells:
- **Type I pneumocytes**: very flat cells that cover about 95% of the surface. Gases pass through them.
- **Type II pneumocytes**: plump, cube-shaped cells that make **surfactant**, a mix of fats and proteins that lowers surface tension so alveoli don't collapse.

Between neighboring alveoli is the **interalveolar septum**, which holds a dense web of **capillaries** plus elastic fibers that help the lung spring back when you exhale.

The **blood-air barrier** is the thin wall gases must cross: type I cell, a shared basement membrane, and the capillary endothelial cell. In its thinnest spots it is only about 0.2-0.5 micrometers thick. Oxygen and carbon dioxide cross it by **diffusion**, moving from high to low concentration.

**Alveolar macrophages** ("dust cells") patrol the air spaces, eating dust and bacteria.

Real example: babies born very early may not yet make enough surfactant. Their alveoli collapse, causing **neonatal respiratory distress syndrome**. Doctors can give artificial surfactant into the airway to help.
levels.college:
Gas exchange begins at the **respiratory bronchioles**, whose walls are interrupted by alveoli, and continues through **alveolar ducts**, **alveolar sacs** and individual alveoli. Adjacent alveoli communicate through **pores of Kohn**, allowing collateral ventilation.

**Alveolar epithelium**
- **Type I pneumocytes (AT1)**: squamous, joined by tight junctions. They are only about 40% of alveolar epithelial cells but cover about 95% of the surface because each is so broad and thin.
- **Type II pneumocytes (AT2)**: cuboidal, often in alveolar corners, with apical microvilli. On electron microscopy they show **lamellar bodies**, concentric stacks of stored surfactant. AT2 cells are also the **progenitors** that divide and turn into AT1 cells after injury.

**Surfactant** is about 90% lipid, mainly **dipalmitoylphosphatidylcholine (DPPC)**, plus surfactant proteins **SP-A, SP-B, SP-C and SP-D**. By the Law of Laplace (P = 2T/r), small alveoli would collapse into larger ones without it. Surfactant lowers surface tension more as an alveolus shrinks, which stabilizes alveoli of different sizes. SP-A and SP-D are collectins that also help with immune defense.

**The interalveolar septum** has a thin side and a thick side:
- Thin side: AT1 cytoplasm, a **fused basement membrane**, and capillary endothelium. Gas exchange happens mainly here.
- Thick side: contains interstitium with fibroblasts, elastic and type I/III collagen fibers. Fluid moves and collects here.

The capillaries are **continuous** (non-fenestrated).

**Alveolar macrophages** come from embryonic precursors and keep renewing themselves locally. Those that have swallowed red blood cells in left heart failure contain hemosiderin and are called **heart failure cells**.

**Fick's law**: diffusion rate is proportional to area times the partial pressure difference, divided by barrier thickness. Disease that thickens the septum (fibrosis) or destroys surface area (emphysema) impairs gas exchange.
levels.phd:
Morphometry by **Weibel** and **Gehr** established the lung's structural numbers. Ochs and colleagues (2004) counted a mean of about 480 million alveoli, with numbers scaling with lung volume. The harmonic mean thickness of the barrier, the value that governs diffusion, is about 0.6 µm in humans. The arithmetic mean is several-fold larger because the thick side contributes more tissue. Weibel's analysis of **symmorphosis** asked whether the lung's diffusing capacity is matched to what the body needs. It found the lung has excess capacity at rest, unlike most links in the oxygen-delivery chain.

**Barrier mechanics.** In the thin side, strength comes mainly from **type IV collagen** in the fused basement membrane. West and Mathieu-Costello showed that high capillary pressure causes **stress failure**: breaks in the endothelium and epithelium. This explains bleeding into the airways in racing horses and part of **high-altitude pulmonary edema**. Fluid is first cleared into the thick-side interstitium and drained by lymphatics near the bronchioles. Fluid only floods the alveoli when this drainage is overwhelmed. AT1 cells actively remove sodium and water through **ENaC** channels, the **Na+/K+-ATPase** pump, and **aquaporin-5** water channels.

**Surfactant biology.** AT2 cells make DPPC in the endoplasmic reticulum. The transporter **ABCA3** loads the lipid into lamellar bodies. SP-B and SP-C are small hydrophobic proteins required to spread the surfactant film. Clements' surface balance experiments in the 1950s and **Avery and Mead's** 1959 study linked surfactant deficiency to hyaline membrane disease. Lack of SP-B is fatal in newborns, while mutations in **SFTPC** or ABCA3 cause interstitial lung disease in children and adults.

**Stem cell niches.** Lineage tracing (Barkauskas et al., 2013) showed AT2 cells are long-term alveolar stem cells. A subset that responds to Wnt signals (**Axin2+**), kept in place by nearby fibroblasts, does most of the repair. When AT2 cells change into AT1 cells, they pass through a transitional state marked by **KRT8** (also called damage-associated transient progenitors). In idiopathic pulmonary fibrosis these cells pile up instead of finishing the switch. That points to failed repair, not just excess fibroblasts, as a driver of fibrosis. A debated question is how much **AT1 cells** can turn back into AT2 cells.
levels.expert:
Clinically, the blood-air barrier explains why **DLCO** (diffusing capacity for carbon monoxide) is a sensitive but nonspecific test. The Roughton-Forster equation splits it into a **membrane conductance** term and a blood term set by **capillary blood volume**. Anemia, pulmonary hypertension and early interstitial lung disease can all lower DLCO even when spirometry is normal. Alveolar bleeding, by contrast, falsely raises it. Correct for hemoglobin before interpreting the result.

**Pathology at the barrier**
- **Diffuse alveolar damage** (the tissue picture of ARDS): an exudative phase with hyaline membranes made of fibrin and dead cell debris lining alveolar ducts. This is followed by a proliferative phase with clusters of AT2 cells. The pattern does not tell you the cause; COVID-19, sepsis, aspiration and drug toxicity look alike.
- **Pulmonary alveolar proteinosis**: alveoli fill with PAS-positive surfactant because macrophages fail to clear it. Most adult cases are autoimmune, caused by antibodies against **GM-CSF**. Treatment uses whole-lung lavage and inhaled GM-CSF; molgramostim showed benefit in the IMPALA trials.
- **Amiodarone lung**: foamy macrophages with lamellar inclusions on electron microscopy, a drug-induced lipid storage problem. Their presence shows exposure, not toxicity.

**Pitfalls**
- In biopsies, collapse from handling and the lung's lack of inflation can make septa look thick, mimicking fibrosis. Inflating the lung with fixative before processing avoids this.
- Repairing AT2 cells can look atypical and be mistaken for adenocarcinoma.

**Recent advances.** Single-cell atlases define two capillary endothelial types: **gCap** cells (general capillary, progenitor-like, aerocyte-supporting) and **aCap** cells, also called **aerocytes**. Aerocytes are very thin and specialized for gas exchange, and they depend on VEGF from AT1 cells (Gillich et al., 2020). Lung organoids and lung-on-chip models now let researchers measure barrier leak directly.

Neuro link for a future neurosurgeon: **neurogenic pulmonary edema** after subarachnoid hemorrhage or severe head trauma comes from a surge of catecholamines that spikes capillary pressure and causes stress failure. It is a direct path from brain injury to damage at the alveolar barrier.

**Open questions**: how fully AT1 cells can regenerate, whether a fibrosis-prone alveolar niche can be reprogrammed, and why repair after COVID varies so widely between people.

keyPoints: Hundreds of millions of alveoli provide about 70-100 m² for gas exchange
Type I pneumocytes are flat and cover ~95% of the alveolar surface
Type II pneumocytes make surfactant (lamellar bodies) and act as alveolar stem cells
Surfactant (mainly DPPC plus SP-A to SP-D) lowers surface tension and prevents collapse
The thin barrier is type I cell, fused basement membrane and capillary endothelium
Alveolar macrophages ('dust cells') clear particles from the air spaces

test.q: Which cell covers about 95% of the alveolar surface?
test.explain: Type I pneumocytes are thin and broad, so although fewer in number, they cover nearly all the surface. Type II cells are plump and cover far less.

test.q: The organelles in type II pneumocytes that store surfactant are:
test.explain: Lamellar bodies are concentric lipid stacks of stored surfactant, seen on electron microscopy.

test.q: What is the main lipid in surfactant?
test.explain: DPPC (dipalmitoylphosphatidylcholine) is the principal phospholipid that lowers surface tension.

test.q: Which layers make up the thin side of the blood-air barrier?
choices: Type I cell, basement membrane, endothelium
Type II cell, elastic fibers, lymphatic vessel
Ciliated cell, lamina propria, smooth muscle
test.explain: Gas crosses the type I cell, a shared (fused) basement membrane, and capillary endothelium.

test.q: Why do premature babies often develop respiratory distress syndrome?
test.explain: Without enough surfactant, surface tension collapses alveoli. Artificial surfactant can help.

test.q: Alveolar macrophages that contain hemosiderin in left heart failure are called:
test.explain: They have eaten leaked red blood cells and store the iron as hemosiderin. Kupffer cells are liver macrophages.

test.q: Openings between neighboring alveoli are called:
test.explain: Pores of Kohn allow collateral air flow between alveoli.

test.q: By Fick's law, which change would most reduce gas diffusion?
test.explain: Diffusion is inversely proportional to thickness, as in fibrosis. The other choices increase or support exchange.

test.q: Which cells act as progenitors that replace type I pneumocytes after injury?
test.explain: Type II cells divide and turn into type I cells during repair.

test.q: Surfactant lowers surface ___, so small alveoli do not collapse.
test.explain: By the Law of Laplace, lower surface tension stabilizes small alveoli.

test.q: What process moves oxygen across the blood-air barrier from high to low concentration?
test.explain: Gas exchange is passive diffusion down partial pressure gradients.

test.q: What is the nickname for alveolar macrophages that eat inhaled particles?
test.explain: Alveolar macrophages are called dust cells because they engulf particles.

kidTest.q: What are alveoli?
choices: Tiny air sacs in the lungs
Tiny bones in the middle ear
kidTest.explain: Alveoli are the little air sacs in the lungs where oxygen and carbon dioxide are exchanged.

kidTest.q: What goes from the air into your blood in the alveoli?
kidTest.explain: Oxygen goes into the blood; carbon dioxide comes out.

kidTest.q: Why is the alveolar wall so thin?
choices: So it can stretch like a balloon
So it can hold more blood
So gases can pass through easily
kidTest.explain: A thin wall lets oxygen and carbon dioxide cross quickly.

kidTest.q: What do the cleaner cells in the alveoli do?
kidTest.explain: They gobble up dust that gets into the lungs.

kidTest.q: Tiny blood tubes wrap around each air bubble. They are called c _ _ _ _ _ _ _ _ _ _.
kidTest.explain: Capillaries are tiny blood vessels that wrap the alveoli.

advancedTest.q: Why is the harmonic mean barrier thickness, not the arithmetic mean, the value used to estimate diffusing capacity?
choices: It includes the thick-side interstitium more strongly
It removes the effect of capillary blood volume
It is easier to measure on light microscopy
It weights thin regions, where most diffusion actually occurs
advancedTest.explain: Diffusion is inversely related to thickness, so thin regions carry most flux. The harmonic mean reflects that, while the arithmetic mean is inflated by the thick side.

advancedTest.q: A patient after subarachnoid hemorrhage develops pulmonary edema. What is the most likely barrier mechanism?
choices: Antibodies against GM-CSF block surfactant clearance
A catecholamine surge raises capillary pressure, causing stress failure
SP-B deficiency prevents the surfactant film from spreading
advancedTest.explain: Neurogenic pulmonary edema reflects a sympathetic surge that raises capillary pressure enough to break the barrier.

advancedTest.q: Recent findings on idiopathic pulmonary fibrosis suggest a central defect is:
choices: Loss of pores of Kohn, blocking collateral airflow
AT2-derived transitional KRT8+ cells failing to become AT1
Overgrowth of type I cells that thicken each septum
Fenestrated capillaries leaking fibrinogen into the interstitium
advancedTest.explain: Transitional cells accumulate instead of finishing differentiation, pointing to failed epithelial repair as a driver.

advancedTest.q: Which finding would raise DLCO rather than lower it?
advancedTest.explain: Blood in the alveoli binds carbon monoxide and falsely raises DLCO. The other findings reduce it.
